title: Coordinating care and transfer of care
blurb: Act as coordinator of care: transfer safely in labour, hand over with the woman at the centre, and pass care seamlessly to the health visitor and GP.
question: Tara is labouring at home when her second stage is delayed. Her community midwife arranges transfer to the obstetric unit. Who should the midwife contact, who travels with Tara, and how should handover happen?

teach.body: Formally, midwives must be able to act as the coordinator of care within interdisciplinary and multiagency teams, arranging a seamless transfer of care when midwifery care is complete (SPM 2.11). In plain English: the midwife is the hub. She makes sure every professional knows what they need to know, the woman is never lost between services, and handovers happen with her, not about her.

teach.caption: NG235 1.5.4: carry out transfer as soon as possible after the decision is made.

teach.h: Handover with the woman at the centre
teach.body: Involve the woman in any handover of care, whether expertise is brought in or a shift ends. It should happen in the room, when appropriate, with her at the centre of the discussion (NG235 1.4.11). During transfer, a midwife who has been involved in her care travels with her, monitoring continues as appropriate, and her birth companion may travel with her if agreed (NG235 1.5.5).

Midwife Lucy explains the delay and the reasons for transfer, and Tara agrees. Lucy calls the ambulance and the obstetric unit's coordinating midwife, who alerts the obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams. Lucy travels with Tara, listening to the fetal heart when safe, while her partner comes too. In the birth room Lucy gives a structured SBAR handover, with Tara included and able to add or correct details.

teach.h: After the birth: handing on care

items.label: Assess both; first void volume; observe 1 effective feed
First midwife visit, face to face, usually at home
First health visitor home visit after midwife care ends
GP postnatal check; infant NIPE examination

teach.caption: NICE NG194 1.1.10, 1.1.14, 1.1.15, 1.2.7.

teach.h: What the health visitor and GP need (NG194 1.1.8)

How the baby is being fed
teach.caption: NG194 1.1.9: the woman or parents are told when care transfers from midwife to health visitor.

teach.text: The 36-hour first visit is a MIDWIFE visit after transfer home from the place of birth (or after a home birth). The 7-to-14-day visit is the HEALTH VISITOR's, counted from transfer out of midwifery care. And if she had no antenatal health visitor visit, consider an extra early one (NG194 1.1.16).

items: SPM 2.11: the midwife coordinates care and arranges seamless transfer when midwifery care ends.
In-labour transfer: call the ambulance and the OU coordinating midwife; a known midwife travels with her.
Handover happens in the room with the woman at the centre; use SBAR.
First midwife visit within 36 hours of transfer home; health visitor visit at 7 to 14 days.
Share complications, mental health, FGM, safeguarding, parental responsibility and feeding at transfer.

summary: You can now coordinate transfer in labour, lead handovers with the woman at the centre, and plan the postnatal handover to health visitor and GP within NICE timeframes. You can also name the information that must travel with her.

A.q: Lola and her baby go home 30 hours after a hospital birth. When should her first postnatal midwife visit take place?
options: Within 36 hours of transfer, face to face, usually at home
Within 72 hours of transfer, by telephone or video call
On day 5, at the same time as the blood spot test
Within 7 to 14 days, at the community clinic
A.why: NG194 1.1.14: the first postnatal midwife visit takes place within 36 hours after transfer from the place of birth, face to face and usually at home.

whyNot.1: 72 hours is too late, and NICE asks for a face-to-face visit.
whyNot.2: Day 5 is the usual blood spot day, not the first visit timing.
whyNot.3: 7 to 14 days is the health visitor's first visit window.

A.q: When does NICE NG194 suggest the first postnatal health visitor home visit should take place?
options: 3 to 5 days after the birth of the baby
28 days after the birth of the baby
At the 6 to 8 week postnatal check
7 to 14 days after transfer from midwifery care
A.why: NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first health visitor home visit 7 to 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care.

whyNot.0: 3 to 5 days falls within the midwife's postnatal care period.
whyNot.1: 28 days would leave a gap after midwifery care ends.
whyNot.2: 6 to 8 weeks is the GP and infant examination timing.

A.q: Before a woman is transferred home from the maternity unit, which assessment does NG194 specifically recommend?
options: Completing the newborn blood spot test
A routine repeat haemoglobin check
Measuring the volume of her first void
Booking her 6 to 8 week GP appointment
A.why: NG194 1.1.10: assess bladder function by measuring the volume of the first void, plus assess both woman and baby and observe at least one effective feed.

whyNot.0: Blood spot sampling is usually on day 5, not before transfer home.
whyNot.1: A routine repeat haemoglobin is not part of NG194 1.1.10.
whyNot.3: The 6 to 8 week check is arranged, but it is not the listed pre-transfer assessment.

B.q: During a home birth, the midwife decides Tara needs transfer for delay in the second stage. Whom should the midwife contact?
options: The ambulance service and the OU coordinating midwife
Tara's GP, who will arrange the hospital admission
The neonatal unit, which will alert the obstetrician
The supervisor of midwives, who will decide on transfer
B.why: NG235 1.5.3: the midwife contacts the ambulance service (if appropriate) and the coordinating midwife in the obstetric unit, who alerts the obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams.

whyNot.1: The GP does not coordinate intrapartum transfer.
whyNot.2: The OU coordinating midwife, not the neonatal unit, alerts the teams.
whyNot.3: Statutory supervision of midwives no longer exists; the attending midwife decides with the woman.

B.q: Grace is labouring at home without complications and requests an epidural. How should the transfer be categorised under NICE NG235?
options: Life-threatening emergency, ambulance category 1
Routine transfer, ambulance category 4
Urgent transfer, ambulance category 2
Planned transfer, booked for the next day
B.why: NG235 1.5.4: categorise as life-threatening (category 1) or urgent, for example for pain relief (category 2).

whyNot.0: Category 1 is for life-threatening emergencies, not pain relief.
whyNot.1: NICE categorises labour transfers as category 1 or 2.
whyNot.3: A woman in labour cannot wait for a next-day transfer.

B.q: At the end of a 12-hour shift, a midwife hands over care of a woman in established labour. How should handover happen?
options: At the midwives' station to protect confidentiality
Outside the room so the woman is not worried
In writing so the incoming midwife can read later
In the room, with the woman at the centre of it
B.why: NG235 1.4.11: involve the woman in any handover of care; it should happen in the room, when appropriate, with the woman at the centre of the discussion.

whyNot.0: Handover away from the woman excludes her from her own care.
whyNot.1: Protecting her from information conflicts with involving her.
whyNot.2: Written notes support but do not replace a face-to-face handover with her.

C.q: The ambulance arrives to transfer Tara from home. The midwife still has equipment to pack. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Send Tara with the crew and follow by car once packed
Travel with Tara and hand over with her involved
Send her notes with the crew and phone the unit
Ask the second midwife, new to Tara, to go with her
C.why: NG235 1.5.5: ensure a midwife who has been involved in her care travels with her, monitoring continues as appropriate, and handover involves the woman.

whyNot.0: The involved midwife should travel with her, not follow.
whyNot.2: Notes and a phone call do not replace an accompanying midwife.
whyNot.3: NICE asks for a midwife involved in her care so far to travel with her.

C.q: On day 12, the midwife is transferring care to the health visitor. The woman has a history of depression and disclosed domestic abuse in pregnancy. What should the midwife do?
options: Omit the abuse disclosure to protect her confidentiality
Ask the woman to tell the health visitor about it herself
Share the mental health and safeguarding information
Wait to share details until after the 6 to 8 week check
C.why: NG194 1.1.8: share previous or current mental health concerns and safeguarding issues when care transfers from midwife to health visitor.

whyNot.0: Safeguarding information must travel with her care; withholding it puts her and the baby at risk.
whyNot.1: Relying on her to pass it on risks loss of vital information.
whyNot.3: Delay leaves the health visitor without essential information at the first visit.

C.q: Ruby did not see a health visitor during pregnancy. What does NICE NG194 suggest when planning her postnatal health visitor care?
options: Delay the first visit until the 6 to 8 week check
Consider an additional early postnatal visit
Arrange contact by telephone in place of a visit
Extend midwife care until the baby is 28 days old
C.why: NG194 1.1.16: if a woman did not receive an antenatal health visitor visit, consider arranging an additional early postnatal health visitor visit.

whyNot.0: Delay would leave a long gap after midwifery care ends.
whyNot.2: NICE suggests an additional visit, not a replacement call.
whyNot.3: Extending midwife care is not the NG194 recommendation.

reteach.title: Passing the baton
reteach.question: In a relay, the baton is dropped at the handover. What makes a maternity handover safe?

blocks.body: In labour: call the ambulance and the OU coordinating midwife, travel with her and hand over in the room with her involved. Going home: assess both, measure the first void, observe a feed, and visit within 36 hours. Leaving midwifery care: tell her, and pass the health visitor everything they need, including mental health, FGM, safeguarding and feeding.

blocks.text: Never let the woman be the messenger for safety-critical information; professionals share it directly.

explain.body: Coordinate care across interdisciplinary and multiagency teams (SPM 2.11). Keep colleagues informed when sharing care (Code 8.3) and share information to identify and reduce risk (Code 8.6). For complex social needs, combine agencies' notes into one plan (CG110 1.2.3).

test.q: Which Code standard asks a midwife to keep colleagues informed when sharing the care of a woman with other professionals?
options: Code 8.3
Code 10.1
Code 13.1
Code 20.2
test.why: Code 8.3: keep colleagues informed when you are sharing the care of individuals with other health and care professionals and staff.

whyNot.1: Code 10.1 concerns completing records at the time or soon after.
whyNot.2: Code 13.1 concerns identifying and assessing signs of normal or worsening health.
whyNot.3: Code 20.2 concerns honesty, integrity and fairness.

explain.body: Base the decision on clinical findings and discuss it with her (1.5.1-1.5.2). Midwife calls the ambulance and OU coordinating midwife (1.5.3). Category 1 if life-threatening, category 2 if urgent (1.5.4). A known midwife travels, monitoring continues, companion may travel (1.5.5).

test.q: Who alerts the obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams when a woman is being transferred in labour?
options: The paramedic crew in the ambulance
The woman's own GP practice
The coordinating midwife in the OU
The woman's chosen birth partner
test.why: NG235 1.5.3: the coordinating midwife in the obstetric unit alerts the relevant professionals.

whyNot.0: The crew transports her; they do not alert hospital teams.
whyNot.1: The GP has no role in intrapartum transfer.
whyNot.3: Partners are not responsible for clinical communication.

explain.body: Before transfer home: assess her health, measure the first void, assess the baby, advise on meconium within 24 hours, and plan feeding including at least one observed effective feed (NG194 1.1.10). Agree timing with her, considering safeguarding (1.1.11-1.1.12). First midwife visit within 36 hours (1.1.14).

test.q: Before a baby goes home, what feeding check does NG194 1.1.10 require as part of the feeding plan?
options: Observing at least one effective feed
Weighing the baby after every feed
A formula top-up before discharge
Two consecutive feeds of 60 mL
test.why: NG194 1.1.10: make sure there is a feeding plan that includes observing at least one effective feed.

whyNot.1: Weighing after feeds is not part of the 1.1.10 check, which asks for an observed effective feed.
whyNot.2: Routine top-ups are not part of NICE guidance.
whyNot.3: No volume target is set for breastfed babies.

explain.body: Communicate the transfer to the health visitor clearly and tell the woman (NG194 1.1.9). Share complications, mental health, FGM, parental responsibility, next of kin, safeguarding and feeding (1.1.8). Health visitor first visit at 7 to 14 days (1.1.15); GP check at 6 to 8 weeks (1.2.7).

test.q: What does NICE NG194 1.1.9 say must happen when care transfers from midwife to health visitor?
options: The GP signs off the transfer form
The baby is weighed by both services
A joint home visit takes place
The woman or parents are told of it
test.why: NG194 1.1.9: the transfer is clearly communicated between professionals, and the woman or parents are informed about it.

whyNot.1: Joint weighing is not a NICE requirement.
whyNot.2: A joint visit is not required by NG194.
